subject: Cloud Computing
title: Data Warehouses in the Cloud
description: A micro-lesson that makes Data Warehouses in the Cloud usable.

hook.text: Your company generates millions of events per day. Where do you store and analyze them? A data warehouse.

buildup.text: Data warehouses — Redshift, BigQuery, Snowflake — are optimized for analytical queries across massive datasets.

discovery.text: They use columnar storage: instead of reading entire rows, they scan only the columns you need. Much faster for queries.

twist.text: Data warehouses are terrible for real-time transactions. They're built for asking questions, not processing orders.

climax.text: Snowflake became a $70 billion company by making cloud data warehousing simpler than anyone else.

punchline.text: Data warehouses answer big questions. Not handle small transactions.

quiz.question: Why do data warehouses use columnar storage?
options: It scans only needed columns instead of entire rows, making analytics faster
Columnar storage is cheaper than row-based storage

details.summary: Cloud data warehouses like Snowflake, BigQuery, and Redshift store and analyze massive structured datasets using SQL. They separate compute from storage, allowing each to scale independently. This architecture enables petabyte-scale analytics at a fraction of on-premises costs.
details.whyItMatters: Data warehouses power business intelligence and analytics. Cloud warehouses eliminated the need for expensive on-premises appliances and made analytics accessible to organizations of all sizes.
takeaways: Compute and storage scale independently for cost efficiency
Optimized for complex analytical queries on large datasets
Snowflake, BigQuery, and Redshift lead the cloud warehouse market

faq.question: How does BigQuery's pricing differ from Redshift?
faq.answer: BigQuery charges per query based on data scanned, with no infrastructure to manage. Redshift charges for provisioned cluster time regardless of queries run. BigQuery suits variable workloads while Redshift can be cheaper for consistent, heavy analytical workloads.

faq.question: What is the difference between a data warehouse and a database?
faq.answer: Operational databases are optimized for fast transactional reads and writes on individual records. Data warehouses are optimized for complex analytical queries scanning millions of rows. They use columnar storage and are not designed for real-time transactional workloads.
